name: First multi-night backpacking trip
summary: Two to five nights on trail, carrying everything. For someone who has day-hiked but never slept out on a backpacking route.

phases.name: Getting ready
phases.summary: Permits, gear and a shakedown hike while there is still time to fix what doesn't work.

phases.name: Last two days
phases.summary: Weather, food, packing and telling someone your plan.

phases.name: On the trail
phases.summary: Walk, water, eat, camp, and look after your feet.

phases.name: Back home
phases.summary: Check in, dry and clean the gear, and note what to change next time.

rules.title: Get the permit as soon as booking opens
rules.detail: Popular routes cap overnight permits per night. Check the land manager's page for when reservations open.

why.text: Quotas fill fast on popular routes, and camping without a permit can mean a fine or being turned around.

rules.title: Break in footwear on long day hikes
rules.detail: At least two hikes of several hours with the loaded pack, in the shoes and socks you will wear.

why.text: Blisters are the most common way a first trip goes wrong, and new shoes rub in places you only find out about hours in.

rules.title: Do a shakedown night close to home
rules.detail: Pitch the tent, cook a meal and sleep in the bag, even in a backyard or campground.

why.text: Finding a missing tent pole or a stove that won't light is cheap at home and miserable on trail.

rules.title: Leave your route and return time with someone
rules.detail: Trailhead, route, campsites, the time to raise the alarm if you haven't checked in, and the ranger station number.

why.text: If you are hurt or lost, rescuers start from what someone at home can tell them. Without it nobody knows to look.

rules.title: Check the forecast and turn back rules
rules.detail: Look at the forecast for the elevations you will reach, and decide in advance what weather makes you turn back.

why.text: Deciding the turnaround before you are tired and committed makes it much easier to actually turn around.

rules.title: Skip cotton next to the skin
rules.detail: Wear synthetic or wool layers and socks.

why.text: Wet cotton stays wet and pulls heat from the body, which is how cool, damp days turn into hypothermia.

rules.title: Treat all water from streams and lakes
rules.detail: Boil it, or filter and then disinfect it, even when it looks clean.

why.text: Clear water can still carry germs that cause days of illness, often starting after you are home.

rules.title: Pack out all trash and food scraps

why.text: Scraps left behind draw animals into campsites. Leave No Trace asks hikers to pack out everything they bring in, food scraps included.

rules.title: Stop at the first hot spot
rules.detail: Tape or cover the spot as soon as it feels warm, before it is a blister.

why.text: Five minutes on a hot spot saves days of limping on a blister.

meds.name: Your regular medications
meds.purpose: Anything you take daily, plus a few extra days in case the trip runs long.
meds.typicalPattern: As usual, with two extra days packed.

why.text: Weather or an injury can add a night, and there is no pharmacy on trail.

meds.name: Pain relief (ibuprofen or paracetamol)
meds.purpose: Sore knees, headaches and aches after long days.
meds.cautions: Ibuprofen is hard on the stomach and kidneys when dehydrated; drink first.

meds.name: Antihistamine
meds.purpose: Insect stings, plant reactions and hay fever.

meds.name: Sunscreen and lip balm with SPF
meds.purpose: Sun protection, one of the ten essentials.
meds.typicalPattern: Morning and again every couple of hours in sun.

why.text: Sun is stronger at altitude and off snow or water, and a burn on day one makes every later day worse.

packing.name: Broken-in hiking boots or trail shoes

obtain.why: They need weeks of breaking in.

why.text: Extra clothing is one of the ten essentials; a shell keeps you dry and blocks wind.

obtain.where: Outdoor shops near popular trailheads often rent
obtain.why: Renting for a first trip avoids buying before you know what you like.

packing.name: Sleeping bag rated for the low temperature

why.text: The ground pulls heat out of you faster than the air does; a good bag on a thin pad still sleeps cold.

obtain.why: It can fly only if it is empty and cleaned of all fuel residue.

why.text: Hot food and boiling water matter most on a cold, wet evening.

obtain.where: An outdoor shop or general store near the trailhead
obtain.why: Fuel can't travel by air, so buy it on arrival and check the shop's hours.
Test it at home; some need assembly or a first flush.

why.text: All backcountry water needs treating.
Phones die and lose signal. Navigation is the first of the ten essentials.

packing.name: Trail food plus one extra day

why.text: A spare day of food is the margin for a delay.

obtain.where: Ranger stations on routes that require one
obtain.why: Required on some routes; rangers often rent them.

why.text: A stomach upset on the drive in is a bad start.

food.name: Trail days
allowed: Calorie-dense snacks every hour or two
avoid: Anything that spoils without a fridge

ideas.name: Instant oats with nut butter and dried fruit
Couscous with olive oil, tuna pouch and spices
ideas.note: Needs only boiling water and five minutes.

ideas.name: Freeze-dried meals
ideas.note: Easy and light, but try one at home first.

why.text: Carrying a pack burns far more than a normal day, and running low on fuel makes you cold and clumsy.

contacts.whenToUse: Permits, trail conditions, and to report an emergency.
Gets your route and calls for help if you miss your return time.

logistics.title: Overnight permit
logistics.detail: Print it or save it offline.

logistics.title: Getting to and from the trailhead
logistics.detail: Car, shuttle or a ride. For a point-to-point route, plan the return leg too.

why.text: Shuttles to remote trailheads can run only a few times a day, and missing the last one is a long walk.

logistics.title: Place to sleep the night before

daily.title: Send route and return time to your check-in person

why.text: Catching rubs at camp keeps tomorrow's walk possible.

daily.title: Tell your check-in person you're out
Dry the tent and sleeping bag

why.text: Gear packed away damp grows mildew within days.
